Single-bus data format is used for communication and synchronization between MCU and
DHT11 sensor. One communication process is about 4ms. Data consists of decimal and integral
parts. Complete data transmission is 40bit, and the sensor sends higher data bit first. Data
format is as follows: 8bit integral RH data + 8bit decimal RH data + 8bit integral T data + 8bit
decimal T data + 8bit checksum. If the data transmission is right, the check-sum should be the
last 8bit of "8bit integral RH data + 8bit decimal RH data + 8bit integral T data + 8bit decimal
T data". When MCU sends a start signal, DHT11 changes from the low-power-consumption
mode to the running mode, waiting for MCU to complete the start signal. Once it is completed,
DHT11 sends a response signal of 40-bit data that include the relative humidity and
temperature information to the MCU. Users can choose to collect (read) some data. Without the
start signal from MCU, DHT11 will not give the response signal to MCU. Once data is
collected, DHT11 will change to the low power-consumption mode until it receives a start

Summarise it easy lang

Here’s a simple summary of that:  

The **DHT11 sensor** uses a **single data line** (single-bus) to talk to the **microcontroller (MCU)**.  
- One full communication takes about **4 milliseconds**.  
- The sensor sends **40 bits** of data in total (from high bit to low bit):  
  → 8 bits: integer part of humidity  
  → 8 bits: decimal part of humidity  
  → 8 bits: integer part of temperature  
  → 8 bits: decimal part of temperature  
  → 8 bits: checksum (for error checking)  

The **checksum** is the sum of the first four data bytes.  
If it matches, the data is valid.  

To start communication, the **MCU sends a start signal**, which wakes up the DHT11.  
Then the sensor responds with the 40-bit data.  
After sending data, the DHT11 goes back to **low-power mode** until the next start signal.

PIRs are made of pyroelectric sensors, a round metal can with a rectangular crystal in the
center, which can detect levels of infrared radiation. Everything emits low-level radiation, and
the hotter something is, the more radiation is emitted. The sensor in a motion detector is split
in two halves. This is to detect motion (change) and not average IR levels. The two halves are
connected so that they cancel each other out. If one-half sees more or less IR radiation than
the other, the output will swing high or low.

Here’s a clear, simple explanation:  

A **PIR (Passive Infrared) sensor** detects **motion** using **infrared radiation** (heat energy) that all objects give off.  

- Inside it, there’s a **pyroelectric sensor** — a small metal can with a **crystal** that reacts to changes in infrared (IR) energy.  
- **Hotter objects** (like humans or animals) give off **more IR radiation**.  
- The sensor is **split into two halves** so it can detect **changes** in IR, not just constant heat.  
- Normally, both halves receive the same amount of IR and cancel each other out, so there’s no signal.  
- When something warm moves in front of the sensor, **one half gets more IR than the other**, causing a difference — this change makes the sensor output a signal, meaning **motion is detected**.

Here’s the straight answer — **when to use PIR vs IR (active infrared) sensors**, and what each is good for 👇  

---

### 🧠 **PIR (Passive Infrared Sensor) — Use Case**
**What it does:** Detects motion of warm objects (like people or animals) by sensing changes in infrared radiation.  
**Doesn’t emit anything**, just senses.

**Use PIR when you need:**
- **Motion detection** — like in security alarms, automatic lights, or home automation.
- **Energy-efficient systems** — it only activates when something moves.
- **Human/animal presence sensing** — e.g., turn on AC when someone enters.

**Examples:**
- Automatic room lights  
- Security motion alarms  
- Smart home presence sensors  
- Outdoor lights that turn on when you walk by  

✅ **Pros:** Cheap, low power, simple, works well for detecting people.  
❌ **Cons:** Can’t detect static (non-moving) objects or measure exact distance.

---

### 🔦 **IR (Active Infrared Sensor) — Use Case**
**What it does:** Uses an **IR LED (emitter)** and a **receiver (photodiode)** to detect **reflected infrared light**.  
It **actively sends** infrared and checks what bounces back.

**Use IR when you need:**
- **Object detection** — e.g., line-following robots, counting objects, obstacle avoidance.  
- **Distance measurement** (short range).  
- **Detecting any surface**, not just warm bodies.

**Examples:**
- Line-follower robots  
- Hand dryers or automatic faucets  
- Obstacle detection in robots  
- Conveyor belt counters  

✅ **Pros:** Works on all kinds of materials (not just warm ones).  
❌ **Cons:** Limited range, can be affected by sunlight or shiny surfaces.

---

### ⚖️ **In short:**
| Feature | PIR | IR (Active) |
|----------|-----|-------------|
| Detects | Heat / Motion | Any object / Surface |
| Emits IR? | No | Yes |
| Best for | People detection | Object detection |
| Detects still object? | ❌ No | ✅ Yes |
| Power use | Low | Moderate |
| Range | Medium (up to ~6m) | Short (a few cm to ~80cm) |

---

👉 **So:**
- Use **PIR** if you want to know **“Is something moving here?”**  
- Use **IR** if you want to know **“Is something in front of me?”**

The working of the IR sensor module is very simple, it consists of two main components: the
first is the IR transmitter section and the second is the IR receiver section. In the transmitter
section, IR led is used and in the receiver section, a photodiode is used to receive infrared
signal and after some signal processing and conditioning, you will get the output.
An IR proximity sensor works by applying a voltage to the onboard Infrared Light Emitting
Diode which in turn emits infrared light. This light propagates through the air and hits an
object, after that the light gets reflected in the photodiode sensor. If the object is close, the
reflected light will be stronger, if the object is far away, the reflected light will be weaker. If
you look closely toward the module. When the sensor becomes active it sends a corresponding
Low signal through the output pin that can be sensed by an Arduino or any kind of
microcontroller to execute a particular task. The one cool thing about this module is that it has
two onboard LEDs built-in, one of which lights on when power is available and another one
turns on when the circuit gets triggered.

avoidance robots. This Sensor is popular among beginners as these are low power, low cost,

Explain

Here’s a clear, easy explanation of how the **IR sensor module** works 👇  

---

### ⚙️ **Basic Working Principle**
An **IR (Infrared) sensor module** has **two main parts**:
1. **Transmitter section** – an **IR LED** that emits infrared light.
2. **Receiver section** – a **photodiode** that detects the reflected infrared light.

When the IR LED sends out invisible infrared light:
- If there’s **no object**, the light just travels away, and nothing is reflected.
- If there **is an object**, the light bounces back and hits the **photodiode**.

The **closer** the object, the **stronger** the reflected light.  
The **farther** the object, the **weaker** the reflection.

---

### 🧩 **Signal Processing**
The **photodiode** converts the reflected infrared light into an electrical signal.  
This weak signal then goes into an **LM358 Op-Amp (comparator)**, which compares it to a reference value.

- If the reflected light is **strong enough**, the Op-Amp output goes **LOW** (triggered).
- If there’s **no reflection**, the output stays **HIGH** (idle).  

This output can be read easily by an **Arduino or any microcontroller** to perform actions (like stopping a robot or turning on an LED).

---

### 💡 **Indicators & Controls**
The IR module has:
- **Power LED** → lights up when the module is powered.  
- **Signal LED** → turns on when the sensor detects an object.  
- **Potentiometer** → used to **adjust sensitivity** (how close or far an object must be to trigger the output).

---

### 🧠 **Main Components Summary**
| Part | Function |
|------|-----------|
| IR LED | Emits infrared light |
| Photodiode | Detects reflected IR light |
| LM358 Op-Amp | Compares signal and gives digital output |
| Potentiometer | Adjusts detection distance/sensitivity |
| Power LED | Shows module is on |
| Signal LED | Shows object detected |
| VCC, GND, OUT pins | Power and signal connections to MCU |

---

### 🔍 **Use Cases**
- Obstacle avoidance robots  
- Object counters  
- Proximity detection (e.g., hand dryers, automatic taps)  
- Line-following robots  

---

### ⚡ **In short:**
The **IR sensor** sends out infrared light → waits for it to bounce back → compares the returned signal → and gives a digital output when an object is detected.  
It’s **simple, cheap, and effective** for close-range object detection.
